label: paragraph_title
text: STUDENT STRIKERS.

label: text
text:
GOVERNMENT'S FIRM ATTITUDE.
SENIORS EXPELLED

label: text
text: The lead which was promised over a month ago on behalf of the Government with regard to striking students will probably be made public at the next meeting of the Board of Education, for the main lines of the Government's attitude have now been decided.

label: text
text: These, the “China Mail” learns officially, are that “strikers” will not be taken back to Government schools, the definition being applied in respect of students who were absent on certain days. As a notice has already appeared in the Chinese Press notifying, on behalf of the Queen's College authorities, that students who were absent on June 17, 18, 19 and 20 need not present themselves for admission it may be deduced that these are the dates considered crucial in respect of other Government Schools.

label: text
text: The Government will "only enforce this expulsion in the case of students of 16 years of age and over, as it is considered that younger students may have absent themselves through intimidation; whereas senior students, after having the position fully explained to them, had no reason to act from motives of fear.

label: text
text: The co-operation among head masters which members of the Board of Education urged as necessary at the last meeting for any measures decided upon to prove effective is, in fact, in being, for a conference of head masters of all local schools was held yesterday at which, the “China Mail” understands, it was agreed that non-Government schools would co-operate in excluding any expelled striking students who might apply for admission. The action taken by such non-Government schools in regard to any of their own students who associated themselves with the strike must of course rest with the head masters of those schools.

label: text
text: "Caution" money will also, it is understood, be required from parents and guardians in the future (also as from the commencement of the next school year). This will be to guarantee the Government against any loss from unwarranted interference with the normal course of study and will be returned after the course of study is complete, providing the conduct of the student in question has been satisfactory.

label: text
text: The fees in respect of Government Schools are to be increased as from the next school year, although the "China Mail" was assured officially that this was not a direct outcome of the strike but merely revision which would be considered necessary in any case.

label: paragraph_title
text: BORDER INCIDENT.

label: text
text: SHUMCHUN STILL HELD BY REDS

label: text
text: As far as can be ascertained from, reliable sources; yesterday morning's fighting at Shumchun was, as already stated, not to have had more than local significance.

label: text
text: Police Headquarters are awaiting the receipt of further details from Lokimachau Station, where the firing was distinctly heard, but the latest news indicates that Shumchun is still in the hands of the Canton Government, and is not controlled by a rival faction as is generally supposed.

label: text
text: The "Red" Government at Canton suspected signs of disloyalty on the part of the troops at Shumchun, and accordingly ordered a commander on the East River to proceed there, with a force and drive them out. This was accomplished yesterday morning when the local troops book to flight after a small engagement with the East River force.

label: text
text: The Whampoa Cadets, numbering about 100, who were near at hand, are reported to have taken no part in the fighting.

text: The large part that pork plays in the dietary of the Chinese has resulted in the pockets of the local Chinese community being considerably affected by the increased prices charged for that commodity. Indignation has been expressed on the grounds that large stocks have recently arrived here and that there is no reason why pork should still be 80 to 90 cents a catty.

label: text
text:
Mr. N. L. Smith, interviewed by a representative of a Chinese newspaper on the matter, said that, and had received complaints in consequence of which he had called the medt merchants into consultation. Their case was that they had not finished killing their old stock which had cost them considerably more than the new, but Mr. Smith, in the interview an question is reported to have stated that he had ordered the merchants to reduce their prices, and such reductions might be expected to take effect in the course of a day or two.
Another matter to which Mr. Smith's attention was called was the temporary re-institution by the Government of the prohibition on the exportation of rice. This prohibition order had again been cancelled and rice could be exported as usual.
I would have pointed this out at the Meeting. I am sure that I voice the feelings of the entire British Community here when I say that we all regret the attack made upon them, and disassociate ourselves with it.

label: text
text: Sir,—Re letter from “Devonian and Lancastrian” on the subject of the remarks made about Americans at the mass meeting on Tuesday evening. I endorse “Devonian and Lancastrian’s” remarks.

text:

Yours, etc.

label: paragraph_title
text: COURT MARTIAL.

label: text
text: ARMY DOCTOR'S EXPLANATION.

label: text
text:
"Is gastritis the same as what is popularly known as 'pains in the stomach'?" asked Captain C.J. F. Bensley, R.A., when cross-examining Captain R.F. Walker, M.C., R.A.M.C., at a District Court Martial at Whitfield Barracks, Kowloon, this morning.
Captain Walker was giving medical evidence as to the results of alcoholic poisoning. He explained that gastritis was in the stomach. People often spoke of stains in the stomach, he continued, when they actually referred to the abdomen and in this was the distinction.

label: text
text: Major W. P. A. Hattersley-Smith, D.S.O., R.A., was President, The other members of the Court were Captain P. H. Drake-Brockman, Surrey Regiment and Lieut. B. R. Wright-Neville, 2nd Punjabis.

label: text
text: Sergeant Samuel Robson, 38th Heavy Battery, R.A., pleaded “not guilty” to a charge of being drunk on August 8 at 10.45 p.m., and a second charge of being unfit for duty for nine days through indulgence in liquor.

label: text
text: Captain Bensley was the prosecutor and Lieut. H.L. C. Hall, R.A., acted as prisoner's counsel.

label: text
text: Battery Sergeant-Major Brice gave evidence that he saw accused helplessly drunk in the sergeants' mess. When accused complained of being ill, Battery Quarter-Master-Sergeant Moore and Lce/Bdr. Dunne helped to remove him to hospital.

label: text
text:
B.Q.M.S. Moore gave cor-
roborative evidence.

label: text
text: Major Pollard, R.A.M.C., of the Kowloon. Military Hospital said that accused was rather excited when he got to hospital, smelt of alcohol and had acute pains in the stomach.

label: text
text: The next day, accused was bent over to the Military Hospital at Bowen Road. There he was treated by Captain Walker who said that the pains complained of were due to alcoholic poisoning. When accused started to cross-examine Captain Walker's discussion, in which Major Hetersley-Smith participated, ensued as to what effect brandy would have on pains in the stomach and as to which specific part of the body was meant when the word "stomach" was used. The query by the prosecutor led to the answer which has already been mentioned.

label: text
text: On oath, accused told the Court that he suffered from chronic indigestion, that his depression was due to trouble at Home, that he had a severe attack of gastritis when coming out on the boat and that his health had been further impaired by the increased consumption of tinned foods since the strike began. On the day in question he felt ill and sent for some brandy. He had reason to believe that the brandy was of very inferior quality, thus causing his condition as he took very little. In reply to the President, accused mentioned the brand. Accused also emphasised his good conduct.

label: text
text: “guilty.” Sentence will be promulgated.
